title: Green oak corner shelf bracket
subtitle: Green-woodwork: a mortise-and-tenon bracket from riven oak
excerpt: A small wall-mounted corner bracket for a shelf, made from two riven green oak pieces joined with a through-tenon and wedge. The green oak carves and chisels easily; the joint tightens as the wood dries. A working piece of furniture made entirely with hand tools.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the mortise-and-tenon green-wood joint; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the through-tenon wedging method.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content.
Split along the grain with a froe and mallet. Riven pieces follow the grain perfectly and are much stronger than sawn equivalents.
A wedge-shaped riving tool driven with a beetle to split a billet along the grain.
A short length of split timber, ready to be worked.

content.text: A corner shelf bracket is two pieces of
riven

oak joined at right angles with a through-tenon and a saw kerf wedge. The horizontal arm (the bracket) has a tenon on its back end; the vertical wall piece has a mortise cut through it to receive the tenon. The tenon is driven through and a wedge sawn into its end causes it to spread inside the mortise and lock the joint. This is a traditional tusk-tenon joint, used across green-woodwork furniture for centuries because it is strong, repairable, and requires no glue. It is the right introduction to mortise-and-tenon work in green oak.
This project uses
green wood
. The
froe
is used to produce the riven section; the tenon is cut with the tenon saw and chisel while the oak is still green and responsive.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
What you need
Wood
Two riven green oak
billets

. Wall piece: 30 cm long, 8 cm wide, 3 cm thick. Bracket arm: 25 cm long, 5 cm wide, 4 cm thick. Oak is the right wood here, it is strong across the grain (the shelf load comes across the grain of the wall piece) and its tannins mean it weathers well if used in a covered outdoor space. Ash is a good substitute for the bracket arm but is weaker than oak when wet.
Tools
Froe and beetle mallet for riving the billets.
Mortise chisel, 9 mm, and carpenter's mallet for cutting the mortise.
Tenon saw for cutting the tenon cheeks and the wedge kerf.
Combination square and marking gauge for layout.
Sloyd knife for refining tenon shoulders.
Leather strop.
Boiled linseed oil.
Workspace
A workbench with a vice, or a solid bench hook clamped to a garden table. The mortise and tenon work needs the wood held very firmly.
The work
Step 1: Rive and flatten the billets
Rive the oak sections from the log. Use the drawknife or sloyd knife with
push cuts
to smooth both flat faces to a consistent thickness. Square the ends with the tenon saw.
Step 2: Mark and cut the tenon

On the back end of the bracket arm, mark a tenon 9 mm wide, centred on the 4 cm thickness, and 6 cm long. Use the marking gauge to set out the cheek lines. Cut the cheeks with the tenon saw, sawing on the waste side of the line. Pare the shoulders clean with the sloyd knife.
Step 3: Mark and chop the mortise

On the wall piece, mark the mortise 5 cm from the top end: 9 mm wide, matching the tenon width, and the full 3 cm depth. Chop the mortise with the mortise chisel, working from both faces inward, clearing waste as you go. Green oak chops cleanly with a sharp chisel and moderate mallet force.
Step 4: Drive the tenon and wedge

Fit the tenon into the mortise. It should go in with hand pressure and a few mallet taps. When the bracket arm is seated at right angles to the wall piece, saw a single kerf down the centre of the tenon end, about 3 cm deep. Whittle a small hardwood wedge from an oak scrap: 3 cm long, tapering from 7 mm to 2 mm. Drive the wedge into the kerf with the mallet. The wedge spreads the tenon inside the mortise and locks the joint.
Finishing

Let the assembled bracket dry for two to three weeks before loading. Apply boiled linseed oil to all surfaces after drying. The joint will have tightened considerably during drying, check the wedge is still firm and tap it a little further if needed. BLO oil rags must be laid flat to dry.
Variations
Double bracket: two arms from one wall piece for a wider shelf.
Angled bracket arm: cut the front end of the bracket arm at 45 degrees for a decorative finish.
Care
Re-oil annually. Check the wedge every two years and re-drive if it has worked loose.

attrs.symptom: The tenon is loose in the mortise after driving
attrs.cause: Tenon is undersize or mortise is oversize, cut on the wrong side of the line
attrs.fix: If the tenon is loose, fit a thin hardwood shim alongside the tenon cheek before driving the wedge. If the mortise is oversize, pack with wood slivers and re-drive the wedge.
